newsitem.title: USA: U.S. retail sales slow in March but still robust.
newsitem.headline: U.S. retail sales slow in March but still robust.

text.p: U.S. retail sales in March slowed from the heated pace of the prior two months but still turned in solid enough gains to keep Federal Reserve officials on the lookout for an overheating economy, analysts said.
While overall retail sales in March were slightly less than expected, analysts focused on the large upward revision to February's already strong overall sales figure.
"I'm a little bit dismayed by the revision to February, although I'm not surprised," said Carol Stone, senior economist at Nomura Securities International Inc in New York.
"Virtually every other economic measure we have gotten for February has been strong," she added.

The Commerce Department said retail sales grew 0.2 percent to a seasonally adjusted $215.6 billion in March and revised February's sales figure to a 1.5 percent gain from a previously reported 0.8 percent rise.
Retail sales grew 5.7 percent in the first quarter of this year, almost double the long-term trend in consumer spending and an unsustainable pace, analysts said.
Excluding autos and light trucks, sales rose 0.5 percent in March versus an upwardly revised 0.9 percent gain in February.

Economists polled by Reuters had expected overall sales to rise 0.6 percent and 0.4 percent ex-autos. Also, a rise in auto sales was also expected after February's robust gain, but a surprise 0.6 percent fall was reported.
The fall in auto sales, which accounts for roughtly a quarter of overall retail sales, was the main factor dragging the headline figure below expectations, analysts said.

"The bottom line is consumption spending exploded in the first quarter. It will moderate in second quarter but do not interpret the moderation as weakness," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA Co).
"It is rare that you can run at 100 miles per hour forever," he added.

Analysts said the report added credence to the argument the Federal Reserve should raise interest rates again at its May 20 policymakers meeting. The Federal Open Market Committee hiked the federal funds rate target 25 basis points to 5.5 percent at its last March 25 meeting.
"There is nothing new in this report for the Federal Reserve or the markets that we didn't know. We had concluded last week after the U.S. employment report that the Fed will tighten," Stone said.
Analysts said the confirmation of a first-quarter spending boom will most likely cause them to upwardly revise their first quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) forecasts.
"It may marginally raise (GDP forecasts) a little bit more -- retail sales was exploding in the first quarter," Strauss said.
Matt Alexy, chief markets strategist at CS First Boston, said the report would "bias the GDP numbers up quite a bit".
Analysts also said a string of recent large revisions by the Commerce Department to past retail sales figures was causing them to doubt the reliabiliity of the data.

The 30-year U.S. Treasury bond fell over half a point after the release of the data. Dealers said the retail sales data, combined with a surprise 0.4 percent jump in core producer prices, edged the Fed closer to another tightening.
In sympathy, the Dow Jones industrials average dived over 60 points in early trade. The dollar held steady against the mark and yen.
((--N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1677))
